subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: In this unit you will learn the words that say where something is. You will use on, under, above, below, behind, in front of and between, and find that the answer can change depending on where you are standing. You will also learn the ordinal numbers from 1st to 10th, and both follow and give position instructions.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 1 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Use position words correctly: on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, next to, between.
Begin to use beside, and start to tell left from right.
Recognise and use ordinal numbers from 1st to 10th.
Say which object is first, last, or a given position in a line.
Follow a simple instruction that uses a position word (‘Put the cup under the mat’).
Give their own position instruction for someone else to follow.
Describe where an object is in relation to another object.
Put everyday events in order using 1st, 2nd, 3rd (a daily routine).
A few small toys or objects you can hold and move: a toy animal, a ball, a cup, a spoon, a stone.
Use everyday distance words (near, far, close) to compare how close or far away things are, and everyday direction words (forward, backward, up, down) to describe how something moves.

concepts.title: On, Under, and the First Position Words
concepts.explanation: Start with the two clearest, most physical words: on and under. These are easy to feel because they involve touch — something rests on a surface, or is tucked under it. Use one object and one surface, and move the object as you name where it is. How to teach it: Put a cup on the mat and say clearly, ‘The cup is on the mat.’ Then move it under the low table: ‘Now the cup is under the table.’ Say the position word a little louder than the rest of the sentence so you hear which word is doing the work. Do this with several objects, then hand the object to you and ask them to place it: ‘Put the stone on the box. Now put it under the box.’ Following your instruction is just as important as saying the word. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Watch. I put the ball ON the chair.” (place it) “Where is the ball?” Child: “On the chair!” You: “Yes! Now I put the ball UNDER the chair.” (place it) You: “Your turn. Put the spoon UNDER the cup.” (child does it) You: “Perfect — under!”
concepts.example: Once on and under are secure, add next to and behind and in front of the same way — one word at a time, always with a real object you can move. Keep using the same clear sentence shape: ‘The ___ is ___ the ___.’ This steady pattern helps a pre-reader hear exactly which word changes.

concepts.title: Above, Below, and Between
concepts.explanation: Above and below are like on and under, but the objects do not touch — the bird is above the tree, high in the sky; the roots are below the ground. Between means right in the middle of two things, so it always needs two objects on either side. How to teach it: Hold a toy bird high over a toy tree and say ‘The bird is above the tree.’ Lower your other hand under the table: ‘My hand is below the table.’ For between, line up two cups and place a single date in the middle: ‘The date is between the two cups.’ make ‘between’ themselves by standing between two chairs, or by putting a stone between two of your own toys. Children sometimes muddle above/below with on/under. Gently point out the difference: on touches, above does not. You do not need you to explain this in words — just to place and point correctly when you ask.
concepts.example: 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Put Teddy BETWEEN the two cups.” (child places it) You: “Yes — in the middle of both!” You: “Now hold your hand ABOVE your head. Is it touching your head?” Child: “No!” You: “That is above — high up, not touching. Well done.”

concepts.title: Position Depends on Where You Stand
concepts.explanation: This is the most important — and trickiest — idea in the unit. Position words like in front of, behind, left and right can change depending on your point of view. What is in front of you may be behind me if we face each other. You naturally think your own view is the only view, so this takes time and gentle demonstration. How to teach it: Stand a toy on the table facing you. Ask, ‘Is the toy in front of you or behind you?’ Then walk around to the other side and ask again from your new spot. Show that the answer changed because you moved, not the toy. Do not rush this. The aim at age five is simply to notice that position can look different from a different place — full mastery comes later.
concepts.example: Left and right are introduced here very gently. Most five-year-olds are only beginning to tell left from right, and many adults still pause to think. Pick your writing or eating hand and name it often: ‘This is your right hand — the hand you hold your spoon with.’ Play simple games — ‘Wave your right hand’, ‘Tap your left knee’ — but treat left and right as a fun start, not a test. It is completely normal for this to take many months.

concepts.title: Ordinal Numbers — 1st to 10th
concepts.explanation: Ordinal numbers tell us which one in an order: first, second, third, and so on. This is different from counting numbers, which tell us how many. Three dates is a quantity; the 3rd date is a position. Children meet ordinal numbers best in real orderings — a line of children, a row of cars, a race, or the steps of the day. How to teach it: Line up five toys or five dates. Point to each in turn from the front and say ‘first, second, third, fourth, fifth.’ Then ask, ‘Which one is third? Point to it.’ Start with just 1st, 2nd and 3rd before stretching to 10th — these first three are the hardest to say and the ones children use most. Lining up the family for a photo, or the children at the masjid, gives a perfect real-life moment to ask ‘Who is first? Who is last?’ A powerful everyday link is the daily routine. Talk through the order of the morning: ‘1st we wake up, 2nd we get dressed, 3rd we wash, 4th we eat.’ Ordering familiar events helps you feel that ordinal numbers describe the sequence of real life, not just toys on a table. 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Here are five dates in a row. Let us find their order. Touch the first one.” You and child: “First, second, third, fourth, fifth.” You: “Now — which date is the 3rd one? Point to it.” Child points. You: “Yes! The third — well done.”
concepts.example: Keep gently separating how many from which one. If you ask ‘How many cars?’ the answer is a count (five). If you ask ‘Which car is red?’ the answer is a position (the 2nd car). Naming both kinds of question out loud helps you feel the difference without needing to explain it.

concepts.title: Following and Giving Position Instructions
concepts.explanation: The real goal of this unit is that you can both follow a position instruction and give one. Understanding grows fastest when you get to be the one in charge. Simple games make this natural and fun. How to teach it: Play a treasure game. Hide a small toy and give one clue at a time: ‘Look under the mat… now look behind the basket.’ Then swap roles — hide the toy and tell you where to look. When you give you an instruction, follow it exactly, even a silly one, so they see that their words truly control what happens. This is also a joyful way to practise ordinal numbers: ‘Take 1st two steps forward, 2nd turn around, 3rd clap your hands.’ A gentle obstacle course is another favourite: crawl under a chair, walk between two cushions, stand behind the box, finish in front of the door. Movement makes the words stick far better than pointing at pictures. Thinking position never changes with viewpoint. You might assume ‘in front of’ is fixed. Walk around the object and show the answer changed because you moved. Believing ‘next to’ means only the right side. ‘Next to’ and ‘beside’ mean either side. Show an object next to another on the left and on the right. Mixing up ordinal and counting numbers. ‘Three cars’ (how many) is not ‘the third car’ (which one). Say both aloud and point to show the difference.
concepts.example: Thinking ‘between’ needs a straight line. Objects can be between others in any arrangement. Show ‘between’ with objects placed in different ways.

concepts.title: Near, Far and Moving Directions
concepts.explanation: Position words are not only about where something is sitting still — they also describe distance (how far away something is) and movement (which way something goes). How to teach it: Stand two toys at different spots — one close to you and one across the room. Ask, 'Which toy is near you? Which toy is far away?' Practise the words near, far and close together using real distances you can walk and feel. Then move to direction of movement: give you simple instructions to act out, such as 'Take two steps forward,' 'Now take one step backward,' 'Reach your hand up,' and 'Now put it down.' Play a simple following game (like a mini 'Simon Says') using forward, backward, up and down so you link the words to your own body moving through space, not just to objects sitting still.
concepts.example: 🗣 Suggested dialogue You: “Put the ball near you, and put the cup far away, across the room.” You: “Which one is closer to you now?” Child: “The ball!” You: “Now let's move. Take two steps forward.” Child: steps forward. You: “Now one step backward.” Child: steps back. You: “You just used direction words with your whole body!”

explorations.title: On, Under, and the First Position Words
explorations.context: Start with the two clearest, most physical words: on and under. These are easy to feel because they involve touch — something rests on a surface, or is tucked under it. Use one object and one surface, and move the object as you name where it is.
explorations.prompt: You put a cup on the mat, then move it under the low table. Where is the cup now?
explorations.hint: Think about whether the cup is resting on top of something or tucked beneath it.
explorations.explanation: Place an object on a surface and say 'on,' then move it beneath the surface and say 'under,' emphasising the position word a little more than the rest of the sentence so it stands out. Because on and under both involve touching, they are the easiest position words to start with before moving to words like above and below, where the objects do not touch.

explorations.title: Above, Below, and Between
explorations.context: Above and below are like on and under, but the objects do not touch — the bird is above the tree, high in the sky; the roots are below the ground. Between means right in the middle of two things, so it always needs two objects on either side.
explorations.prompt: A bird flies high above a tree without ever touching it. Which word describes the bird's position — above or below?
explorations.hint: Above means higher up without touching; below means lower down without touching.
explorations.explanation: Above and below work like on and under but without any touching — a bird above a tree is high in the sky, while something below the ground is out of sight beneath it. Between needs two objects, one on each side, so line up two items with a gap and place a third thing in the middle to show the word in action.

explorations.title: Position Depends on Where You Stand
explorations.context: This is the most important — and trickiest — idea in the unit. Position words like in front of, behind, left and right can change depending on your point of view. What is in front of you may be behind me if we face each other.
explorations.prompt: A toy sits on the table facing you, so it looks like it is in front of you. Now walk around to the other side of the table and look again — is it still in front of you?
explorations.answer: No — once you're on the other side, the toy is now behind you, because in front of and behind depend on where you are standing.
explorations.hint: Position words like in front of and behind change depending on which side you are standing on.
explorations.explanation: Look at that words like in front of, behind, left and right depend on where you are standing — an object in front of you may be behind you if you are facing each other across a table. Walking around an object together and asking the same question from each new spot helps you see that position is relative, not fixed.

explorations.title: Ordinal Numbers — 1st to 10th
explorations.context: Ordinal numbers tell us which one in an order: first, second, third, and so on. This is different from counting numbers, which tell us how many. Three dates is a quantity; the 3rd date is a position.
explorations.prompt: Five toys are lined up in a row. Counting from the front — first, second, third, fourth, fifth — which position is the middle toy in?
explorations.answer: 3rd — the middle toy, with two toys before it and two after it.
explorations.hint: Point to each toy in turn from the front and count: first, second, third.
explorations.explanation: Line up several objects and point to each one in turn from the front, saying 'first, second, third' and so on — ordinal numbers tell us which position something holds, not how many there are. Everyday routines, like the order of getting up, washing, and eating breakfast, give you a natural place to practise 1st, 2nd, and 3rd.

explorations.title: Following and Giving Position Instructions
explorations.context: The real goal of this unit is that you can both follow a position instruction and give one. Understanding grows fastest when you get to be the one in charge. Simple games make this natural and fun. How to teach it: Play a treasure game.
explorations.prompt: You are hiding a toy for your friend to find and give the clue, 'Look under the mat.' Where should your friend look first?
explorations.hint: Follow the position word in the clue exactly — it tells you exactly where to look.
explorations.explanation: Give you one position clue at a time, such as 'look under the mat,' and watch them act it out before offering the next clue — following a real instruction makes the words stick far better than naming positions in a picture. Then swap roles so you give you an instruction to follow, which shows them they truly understand a word by being able to use it themselves.

explorations.title: On, Under, and the First Position Words
explorations.context: Start with the two clearest, most physical words: on and under. These are easy to feel because they involve touch — something rests on a surface, or is tucked under it. Use one object and one surface, and move the object as you name where it is.
explorations.prompt: A bird is flying higher than a nest, without touching it. Should you circle 'above' or 'below'?
explorations.hint: Check whether the bird is higher or lower than the nest, and remember it isn't touching it.
explorations.explanation: Look at where the bird is compared to the nest — since it is higher up and not touching the nest, the correct word is above, not below. Pointing up for 'above' and down for 'below' as you say each word helps a pre-reader feel the difference in their body, not just hear it.

methods.title: Naming On and Under
methods.example: A date on a plate, then a date under the plate
steps: Place a date on top of a plate and say clearly, 'The date is ON the plate.'
Move the date underneath the plate and say, 'Now the date is UNDER the plate.'
Put a stone on a stool, then under the stool, naming the position aloud each time.

methods.title: Naming Above, Below and Between
methods.example: A kite above a roof, a well below the ground, a date between two cups
steps: Hold a toy or picture of a kite high above a roof and say, 'The kite is ABOVE the roof.'
Point to a well or a hole in the ground and say, 'The water is BELOW the ground.'
Line up two cups with a gap between them, place one date in the gap, and say, 'The date is BETWEEN the two cups.'

methods.title: Finding Front, Behind, Left and Right
methods.example: A toy goat facing you, then facing the parent from across the table
steps: Stand a toy goat on the table facing you and ask, 'Is the goat in front of you or behind you?'
Walk around to the other side of the table and ask the same question again from your new spot, showing that the answer changes.
Point to your writing or eating hand and name it 'right' (or 'left'), repeating this often during everyday play.

methods.title: Naming Next to and Beside
methods.example: A spoon placed right beside a cup
steps: Place a spoon so it touches the side of a cup, not on top and not underneath, and say, 'The spoon is NEXT TO the cup.'
Move a button so it touches the other side of the cup and say, 'The button is BESIDE the cup too.'
Put a stone next to a bowl and describe where they placed it.

methods.title: Counting in Order: 1st to 10th
methods.example: Five dates lined up in a row
steps: Line up five dates (or five stones) in a row and point to each one from the front, saying 'first, second, third, fourth, fifth.'
Ask yourself, 'Which one is third?' and have them point to it before you confirm.
Rearrange the dates and repeat the counting so you practise naming each ordinal position, not just memorising the order.

methods.title: Following and Giving Position Instructions
methods.example: Hiding a button under a mat or behind a basket
steps: Hide a small button and give one clue at a time, such as 'Look under the mat.'
Follow the clue exactly, then give a second clue, such as 'Now look behind the basket.'
Swap roles so you hide the button and gives you a position clue to follow, checking that their instruction makes sense.

workedExamples.title: On and Under: The Bottle Cap
workedExamples.prompt: Duniya puts a bottle cap on a stool, then moves it under the stool. Which word describes where the bottle cap is now?
workedExamples.solution: Start with the bottle cap resting on top of the stool — that position is 'on'. Duniya then moves it underneath the stool, so it now touches the floor beneath the stool. Because it is tucked beneath the stool, the correct word is 'under'.

workedExamples.title: Above and Below: The Kite and the Roof
workedExamples.prompt: A kite flies above the roof, and a well of water is below the ground. Which word tells us where the kite is compared to the roof?
workedExamples.solution: The kite is high in the sky, higher than the roof, and it never touches the roof — that is 'above'. The well of water is lower than the ground's surface and out of sight — that is 'below'. Point up to show 'above' and point down to show 'below' so you feel the difference.

workedExamples.title: In Front of and Behind: The Goat and the Hut
workedExamples.prompt: A goat stands facing the door of a hut. Is the goat in front of the hut or behind it?
workedExamples.solution: Walk around the hut with you and show that the side with the door is the front. Since the goat stands facing the door, it is on the front side of the hut, so it is 'in front of' the hut. If the goat walked around to the wall with no door, it would be 'behind' the hut.

workedExamples.title: Next to the Bucket
workedExamples.prompt: A stone is placed right next to a bucket, touching its side. What position word describes the stone?
workedExamples.solution: Place a stone so it touches the side of a bucket, not on top and not underneath. Because it is alongside the bucket, at the same level, the correct word is 'next to' — you can also say 'beside'. Practise by placing a spoon next to a cup and naming it together.

workedExamples.title: Between Two Cups
workedExamples.prompt: Two cups sit on the table with one date placed exactly in the middle of them. Where is the date?
workedExamples.solution: Line up two cups with a gap between them and place one date in the gap. Because the date has a cup on its left and a cup on its right, it sits in the middle of the two objects, so the correct word is 'between'.

workedExamples.title: Above the Nest
workedExamples.prompt: ★ 🐦 above a nest 🪺. Circle: above / below
workedExamples.solution: Look at the picture: the bird is flying higher than the nest and is not touching it. Because it is higher up without touching, the correct word to circle is 'above', not 'below'.

workedExamples.title: Below the Boat
workedExamples.prompt: ★ 🐟 below a boat ⛵. Circle: above / below
workedExamples.solution: The fish swims in the water, lower than the boat floating on the surface. Since the fish is lower down and does not touch the boat, the correct word to circle is 'below'.

workedExamples.title: In Front of the House
workedExamples.prompt: ★ 🐕 in front of a house 🏠. Circle: behind / in front of
workedExamples.solution: The dog stands on the side of the house where the door is, facing towards it. Because that is the entrance side, the correct word to circle is 'in front of', not 'behind'.

workedExamples.title: Between the Carrots
workedExamples.prompt: ★ 🐇 between two carrots 🥕 🥕. Circle: next to / between
workedExamples.solution: The rabbit sits with one carrot on its left and one carrot on its right. Because it has a carrot on both sides, the correct word to circle is 'between', not 'next to'.

workedExamples.title: Finding the 2nd Goat in Line
workedExamples.prompt: Four goats stand in a line: a brown goat, a white goat, a black goat, and a spotted goat, in that order. Which goat is 2nd in the line?
workedExamples.solution: Point to each goat from the front of the line and count: 'first the brown goat, second the white goat, third the black goat, fourth the spotted goat.' The goat in the second position is the white goat.

workedExamples.title: Ordering the Train Carriages
workedExamples.prompt: Here is a train: 🚂 🟥 🟦 🟩 🟨 🟪. Which colour carriage is 3rd after the engine?
workedExamples.solution: Count the carriages after the engine in order: 1st is red, 2nd is blue, 3rd is green, 4th is yellow, 5th is purple. So the 3rd carriage is green.

workedExamples.title: The 3rd Carriage
workedExamples.prompt: The engine 🚂 is 1st, the red carriage 🟥 is 2nd, and the blue carriage 🟦 is 3rd. Which carriage is 3rd?
workedExamples.solution: Say the order aloud while pointing: 'The engine is first, the red carriage is second, the blue carriage is third.' Because the blue carriage comes right after the red one, it is 3rd.

practice.prompt: Duniya puts a bottle cap on a stool, then moves it under the stool. Which word describes where the bottle cap is now?
practice.answer: Under (the bottle cap is now beneath the stool).
practice.hint: Ask whether the bottle cap is resting on top of the stool or tucked beneath it.

practice.prompt: A kite flies above the roof, and a well of water is below the ground. Which word tells us where the kite is compared to the roof?
practice.answer: Above (the kite is higher than the roof and does not touch it).
practice.hint: Above means higher up without touching; below means lower down without touching.

practice.prompt: A goat stands facing the door of a hut. Is the goat in front of the hut or behind it?
practice.answer: In front of the hut (it faces the door, on the entrance side).
practice.hint: The front of a building is usually the side with the door or entrance.

practice.prompt: A stone is placed right next to a bucket, touching its side. What position word describes the stone?
practice.hint: Next to and beside both mean right alongside something, not on top or underneath.

practice.prompt: Two cups sit on the table with one date placed exactly in the middle of them. Where is the date?
practice.hint: Between means an object has something on both sides of it.

practice.prompt: ★ 🐦 above a nest 🪺. Circle: above / below
practice.answer: Above (the bird is higher than the nest, not touching it).
practice.hint: Check whether the bird is higher or lower than the nest.

practice.prompt: ★ 🐟 below a boat ⛵. Circle: above / below
practice.answer: Below (the fish is lower than the boat, under the water).
practice.hint: The fish is in the water — is that higher or lower than the boat?

practice.prompt: ★ 🐕 in front of a house 🏠. Circle: behind / in front of
practice.answer: In front of (the dog stands on the entrance side of the house).
practice.hint: Look for the door of the house — the dog is on that side.

practice.prompt: ★ 🐇 between two carrots 🥕 🥕. Circle: next to / between
practice.answer: Between (the rabbit has a carrot on each side).
practice.hint: Count the carrots on each side of the rabbit — how many sides have a carrot?

practice.prompt: Four goats stand in a line: a brown goat, a white goat, a black goat, and a spotted goat, in that order. Which goat is 2nd in the line?
practice.answer: The white goat (2nd in the line).
practice.hint: Start counting from the front of the line: first, second, third, fourth.

practice.prompt: Here is a train: 🚂 🟥 🟦 🟩 🟨 🟪. Which colour carriage is 3rd after the engine?
practice.hint: Count the carriages one at a time after the engine: first, second, third.

practice.prompt: The engine 🚂 is 1st, the red carriage 🟥 is 2nd, and the blue carriage 🟦 is 3rd. Which carriage is 3rd?
practice.hint: Point to each part of the train in order and count: 1st, 2nd, 3rd.

activities.title: Practise together
activities.materials: Paper, pencil and familiar household objects
steps: Choose one idea from this unit.
Build or draw a model of it.
Explain your model to a family member.
Write one question of your own and solve it.

rules.title: Near, Far and Moving Directions
rules.text: Position words are not only about where something is sitting still — they also describe distance (how far away something is) and movement (which way something goes).

terms: On top of, or underneath, something
Higher than, or lower than (not touching)
At the back of, or at the front of
In the middle of two things
The very front, or the very end, of an order
A number that tells position, not how many
commonMistakes: Children often skip an event when counting order
Say each action aloud while holding up a finger for every step so the count matches the actions.
Children sometimes say 'between' when only one object is nearby. Between needs two objects, one on each side
Next to just needs one neighbour.
Children sometimes point to the date being 'next to' one cup only. Ask them to check both sides
Between needs a neighbour on each side.
Children sometimes circle 'above' by mistake because the fish is drawn moving upward in the picture
Point out that the fish is still under the water, lower than the boat.
Children sometimes circle 'behind' if the dog is drawn small or far away. Remind them that distance does not matter
Only which side of the house the dog is on.

fluency.prompt: Duniya puts a bottle cap on a stool, then moves it under the stool. Which word describes where the bottle cap is now?
fluency.answer: Under (the bottle cap is now beneath the stool).
fluency.hint: Ask whether the bottle cap is resting on top of the stool or tucked beneath it.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children often keep saying 'on' out of habit even after the object has moved. Ask them to point to where the object is now before naming the position word.

fluency.prompt: A kite flies above the roof, and a well of water is below the ground. Which word tells us where the kite is compared to the roof?
fluency.answer: Above (the kite is higher than the roof and does not touch it).
fluency.hint: Above means higher up without touching; below means lower down without touching.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes confuse 'above' with 'on' because both can mean 'higher'. Remind them: above never touches, on always touches.

fluency.prompt: A goat stands facing the door of a hut. Is the goat in front of the hut or behind it?
fluency.answer: In front of the hut (it faces the door, on the entrance side).
fluency.hint: The front of a building is usually the side with the door or entrance.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children often judge front/behind only from their own position, not the building's entrance. Show the door first, then decide front and behind from there.

fluency.prompt: A stone is placed right next to a bucket, touching its side. What position word describes the stone?
fluency.hint: Next to and beside both mean right alongside something, not on top or underneath.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes say 'between' when only one object is nearby. Between needs two objects, one on each side — next to just needs one neighbour.

fluency.prompt: Two cups sit on the table with one date placed exactly in the middle of them. Where is the date?
fluency.hint: Between means an object has something on both sides of it.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes point to the date being 'next to' one cup only. Ask them to check both sides — between needs a neighbour on each side.

fluency.prompt: ★ 🐦 above a nest 🪺. Circle: above / below
fluency.answer: Above (the bird is higher than the nest, not touching it).
fluency.hint: Check whether the bird is higher or lower than the nest.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes circle 'below' because the nest is drawn underneath the bird in the picture. Remind them to focus on where the bird itself is, not the nest.

fluency.prompt: ★ 🐟 below a boat ⛵. Circle: above / below
fluency.answer: Below (the fish is lower than the boat, under the water).
fluency.hint: The fish is in the water — is that higher or lower than the boat?
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes circle 'above' by mistake because the fish is drawn moving upward in the picture. Point out that the fish is still under the water, lower than the boat.

fluency.prompt: ★ 🐕 in front of a house 🏠. Circle: behind / in front of
fluency.answer: In front of (the dog stands on the entrance side of the house).
fluency.hint: Look for the door of the house — the dog is on that side.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes circle 'behind' if the dog is drawn small or far away. Remind them that distance does not matter — only which side of the house the dog is on.

fluency.prompt: ★ 🐇 between two carrots 🥕 🥕. Circle: next to / between
fluency.answer: Between (the rabbit has a carrot on each side).
fluency.hint: Count the carrots on each side of the rabbit — how many sides have a carrot?
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes circle 'next to' because they only notice one carrot at a time. Ask them to check both sides of the rabbit before choosing.

fluency.prompt: Four goats stand in a line: a brown goat, a white goat, a black goat, and a spotted goat, in that order. Which goat is 2nd in the line?
fluency.answer: The white goat (2nd in the line).
fluency.hint: Start counting from the front of the line: first, second, third, fourth.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes count from the back of the line instead of the front. Always start counting 'first' from the front of the line or queue.

fluency.prompt: Here is a train: 🚂 🟥 🟦 🟩 🟨 🟪. Which colour carriage is 3rd after the engine?
fluency.hint: Count the carriages one at a time after the engine: first, second, third.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes count the engine itself as '1st carriage'. Remind them the engine leads the train — counting of carriages starts after the engine.

fluency.prompt: The engine 🚂 is 1st, the red carriage 🟥 is 2nd, and the blue carriage 🟦 is 3rd. Which carriage is 3rd?
fluency.hint: Point to each part of the train in order and count: 1st, 2nd, 3rd.
fluency.errorFeedback: Children sometimes mix up 2nd and 3rd when colours are involved. Have them point and say the ordinal word aloud for each carriage before answering.

realProblems.prompt: At home, Amina washes her hands, then eats anjero, then brushes her teeth. Put these three steps in order: 1st, 2nd, 3rd.
realProblems.answer: 1st: wash hands, 2nd: eat anjero, 3rd: brush teeth.
realProblems.hint: Think about what Amina does first thing, and what she does right at the end.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children sometimes order events by which they like best rather than which happens first. Retell the story in order and ask 'what happens first?' before assigning numbers.

realProblems.prompt: At the market, five women are standing in a line to sell dates. Fatima is 3rd in the line. How many women are standing in front of Fatima?
realProblems.answer: 2 women are in front of Fatima (1st and 2nd).
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children often confuse '3rd in line' with '3 people in front'. Show the line physically and count only the people before Fatima, not including her.

realProblems.prompt: A bus stops at 4 villages on its journey: Village A is 1st, Village B is 2nd, Village C is 3rd, and Village D is 4th. Which village does the bus reach last?
realProblems.answer: Village D, because it is 4th and the last stop.
realProblems.hint: The last stop is the one with the highest ordinal number in this journey.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children sometimes think 'last' means the biggest village rather than the final position in order. Point along the route and count the stops in order to find the last one.

realProblems.prompt: Before bed, put your shoes under your bed and your book next to your pillow. Where did you put the book?
realProblems.hint: Look for the position word right before 'pillow' in the instruction.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children may mix up which object goes with which position word when two instructions are given together. Repeat one instruction at a time and have you act it out before moving to the next.

realProblems.prompt: In the morning, Hodan wakes up, then prays, then gets dressed, then eats breakfast. What is she doing 3rd?
realProblems.hint: Count through the morning events in order: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children often skip an event when counting order. Say each action aloud while holding up a finger for every step so the count matches the actions.

realProblems.prompt: At dinner, the plate is between the cup and the spoon. The cup is on the left of the plate. Where is the spoon?
realProblems.answer: The spoon is on the right side of the plate.
realProblems.hint: If the plate is between two things, one is on each side of it.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Children sometimes think 'between' names only one neighbour. Show physically: place three objects in a row and ask which one is between the other two.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Look at a picture of a fish swimming below a boat, not touching it. Explain why we say the fish is below the boat and not on the boat or above the boat.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The fish is in the water, lower than the boat, so we say it is below the boat. It is not on the boat, because on means touching the top surface. It is not above the boat either, because above means higher up, like a bird in the sky. Below tells us the fish's position is lower, without touching.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A dog is standing in front of a house, facing the door. Explain why we say the dog is in front of the house and not behind it or beside it.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The dog is on the side of the house where the door and entrance are, and it is facing towards it, so we say it is in front of the house. If the dog were on the far side, out of sight, we would say it is behind the house. If the dog stood right next to a wall instead of facing the entrance, we would say it is beside the house.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A rabbit is sitting between two carrots, with one carrot on each side. Explain why we say the rabbit is between the carrots and not next to just one of them.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Between means the rabbit has something on both sides — one carrot on the left and one carrot on the right. If the rabbit had only one carrot beside it, we would say the rabbit is next to that carrot. Because there are two carrots, one on each side, between is the correct word.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Ordinal Numbers — 1st to 10th.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Ordinal numbers tell us which one in an order: first, second, third, and so on. This is different from counting numbers, which tell us how many. Three dates is a quantity; the 3rd date is a position. Children meet ordinal numbers best in real orderings — a line of children, a row of cars, a race, or the steps of the day.

How to teach it: Line up five toys or five dates. Point to each in turn from the front and say ‘first, second, third, fourth, fifth.’ Then ask, ‘Which one is third? Point to it.’ Start with just 1st, 2nd and 3rd before stretching to 10th — these first three are the hardest to say and the ones children use most. Lining up the family for a photo, or the children at the masjid, gives a perfect real-life moment to ask ‘Who is first? Who is last?’

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Following and Giving Position Instructions.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The real goal of this unit is that you can both follow a position instruction and give one. Understanding grows fastest when you get to be the one in charge. Simple games make this natural and fun. How to teach it: Play a treasure game. Hide a small toy and give one clue at a time: ‘Look under the mat… now look behind the basket.’ Then swap roles — hide the toy and tell you where to look. When you give you an instruction, follow it exactly, even a silly one, so they see that their words truly control what happens. This is also a joyful way to practise ordinal numbers: ‘Take 1st two steps forward, 2nd turn around, 3rd clap your hands.’

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in On, Under, and the First Position Words.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Start with the two clearest, most physical words: on and under. These are easy to feel because they involve touch — something rests on a surface, or is tucked under it. Use one object and one surface, and move the object as you name where it is. How to teach it: Put a cup on the mat and say clearly, ‘The cup is on the mat.’ Then move it under the low table: ‘Now the cup is under the table.’ Say the position word a little louder than the rest of the sentence so you hear which word is doing the work. Do this with several objects, then hand the object to you and ask them to place it: ‘Put the stone on the box. Now put it under the box.’ Following your instruction is just as important as saying the word.

selfAssessment: I can use position words correctly: on, under, above, below, behind, in front of, next to, between.
I can begin to use beside, and start to tell left from right.
I can recognise and use ordinal numbers from 1st to 10th.
I can say which object is first, last, or a given position in a line.
I can follow a simple instruction that uses a position word (‘Put the cup under the mat’).
I can give their own position instruction for someone else to follow.
I can describe where an object is in relation to another object.
I can put everyday events in order using 1st, 2nd, 3rd (a daily routine).
